name: Executive order of November 4, 1873 enlarging the Quinault Reservation (same order as cession-1873-11-04-quillehute-quinaielt)
promises: The President set apart an enlarged reserve north and east of the treaty reserve, up to Quinault Lake and the Queets River, for the Quinaielt, Quillehute, Hoh, Quit and other fish-eating Indians of the Pacific coast.

breaches.what: The Court of Claims held that the northern boundary of the reservation had been located wrongly: the "northwest point" of Quinault Lake named in the 1873 order is the point farthest north on its western shore, and the United States had taken the lands lying between the correct line and the line it adopted. The court found the line used was adopted from a consideration of expediency only, quoting the Commissioner of Indian Affairs' letter noting that white settlers had located on the land.
breaches.whoFoundIt: Court of Claims, The Quinaielt Tribe of Indians v. United States, 102 Ct. Cl. 822 (1945)

source.title: The Quinaielt Tribe of Indians v. The United States, 102 Ct. Cl. 822 (February 5, 1945)
source.publisher: Caselaw Access Project, Harvard Law School

breaches.what: Valuing the taking, the Court of Claims found that the United States took the 15,928.87 acre tract between 1892, when the erroneous survey was completed, and March 1, 1898, when the remaining land went into the national forest reserve or to the State of Washington. It valued the land at $25,000 and, with interest, found $87,988.68 due, but then set off $87,995.62 the United States had spent for the tribes outside treaty obligations, and dismissed the petition.

landTaken: The Court of Claims found a tract of 15,928.87 acres west of Quinault Lake taken on various dates between 1892 and March 1, 1898; an Act of June 4, 1897 (30 Stat. 11, 34) withdrew the remainder of the tract from entry (118 Ct. Cl. 220).
compensation: None. The Court of Claims valued the land at $25,000 and found $87,988.68 due with interest, then set off $87,995.62 in federal spending for the tribes and dismissed the petition in 1951 (118 Ct. Cl. 220).
today: This record is the same executive order as cession-1873-11-04-quillehute-quinaielt; see that file for the full record.

openQuestions: Duplicate of cession-1873-11-04-quillehute-quinaielt (Royce area 551). Royce's note for the 1873 order says "See 372"; area 372, which this record maps, is the original reserve of the 1855-1856 Treaty of Olympia, so this record's map area is not land the 1873 order added. treaties.json should probably merge the two records.

Audit 2026-11-08: both Court of Claims opinions re-opened (102 Ct. Cl. 822, decided February 5, 1945; 118 Ct. Cl. 220, decided January 9, 1951); every figure and date in the breaches matches. Reworded the 1945 breach: the white-settler reason is the Commissioner of Indian Affairs' letter, which the court quoted, not the court's own finding.

Audit 2026-11-08: the 1945 opinion says the 1873 order was issued "formally designating the reservation as provided for by the Treaty" and included Superintendent Miller's 1861 reserve, so this is the treaty reservation selected under the Treaty of Olympia, not a reservation made only by executive order; Jordan's executive-order rule does not apply. The two 1873-11-04 records now carry the same breaches, landTaken and compensation.

plain.promised: In 1873 the President enlarged the Quinault Reservation for the Quinault, Quileute, Hoh, Queets and other coast peoples.
plain.happened: The northern line was surveyed in the wrong place. The Court of Claims held in 1945 that the United States had taken 15,928.87 acres.
plain.today: In 1951 the court valued the land at $25,000, then subtracted federal spending for the tribes and dismissed the claim, so nothing was paid.
